title: Literary Analysis and Interpretation
notes: Analysis names what is on the page: diction, image, structure, and speaker. Interpretation says what those choices do for meaning. Keep the two moves separate so a reading stays tied to the text.

Start with the title and the speaker. Mark one striking word or image, then describe the form: line length, repetition, or a shift in tone. Only after that, state a meaning and quote the line that supports it.
Theme is the idea the text keeps returning to. Tone is the speaker's attitude toward the subject. A theme such as loss needs a tone such as bitter or resigned, each backed by a phrase from the text.
Two interpretations can both be possible. Prefer the one that accounts for more of the text and does not ignore a clear contradiction. Say which lines the weaker reading leaves out.
A story that ends with an open door: analysis records the image. Interpretation might call it freedom or unfinished danger. The stronger reading uses earlier scenes, not the last image alone.
